p.x:
Two years ago, Mai started a small company. She makes bags from old rice sacks and sells her products online. At first, she worked alone at home. She took photos of the bags, designed a simple logo and posted adverts on social media.
In the first month, she sold only five bags. But Mai didn't give up. She asked customers what they liked and changed her designs. Slowly, the number of orders grew. Now her sales are much higher, and she makes a small profit every month. Last year she found a business partner, her friend Joy, who helps with the shop.
Mai has big plans. She wants to open a real shop in Chiang Mai and export her goods to Japan. "It's hard work," she says. "Some months we close with a loss, but I love what I do."

When the Thai company Green Leaf decided to launch a new iced tea, the marketing team had a big challenge. The market was already full of similar drinks, and their main competitor had a much bigger budget.
First, they did a survey of 2,000 people to understand demand. The results showed that young people wanted healthier drinks with less sugar. So the team chose students and young office workers as their target group. They created a short, catchy slogan: "Less sugar, more life." Instead of paying for TV adverts, they decided to advertise mainly on social media and at university events.
There were problems too. The special tea leaves had to be imported from Japan, and when the supply was delayed, some shops ran out of stock. A few angry customers complained online, and the company worried about its reputation. However, the team responded quickly and opened a new branch office in Chiang Mai to handle northern orders. Within six months, the drink was one of the best-selling in the country.

Many of today's biggest companies began as tiny startups run by a few friends. What turns a small idea into a global business? Experts point to several factors.
The first is finding a niche: a specific need that larger companies have ignored. By focusing on a small group of customers, a startup can build loyalty before expanding. The second is money. Most young companies need investors to survive the early years, when costs are high and revenue is low. In exchange, investors receive shares, becoming shareholders who expect the company to grow.
As companies grow, their strategy often changes. Many outsource manufacturing to countries with lower costs and move their headquarters to major business centres. Large advertising campaigns help build a global brand. Some companies grow by merger, joining with competitors to become even bigger.
However, success can create new problems. When one company controls most of a market, it may become a monopoly, able to raise prices and limit competition. Governments in many countries now investigate tech giants to ensure that consumers are protected and that new startups still have a fair chance.
